en.title: Medical Laboratory Science: the whole course
en.short: What medical laboratory science is, how the degree is organised, its main areas and how to study it.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text: These notes teach concepts in medical laboratory science. They are not medical advice and do not replace teachers, textbooks, laboratory protocols or official guidelines. They do not give drug doses. Guidelines change and differ between countries, so check current national or World Health Organization (WHO) guidance. Work in a laboratory only under supervision and follow local safety and quality rules. Test results affect care, so accuracy, confidentiality and ethics matter.

sections.heading: What medical laboratory science is
sections.text:
Medical laboratory science is the health profession that performs and interprets laboratory tests on blood, urine, stool, tissue, swabs and other specimens. Results support screening, diagnosis, treatment, monitoring and public health surveillance. The work is not only operating machines. It includes choosing the right test, collecting and handling specimens correctly, running quality control, recognising interference, interpreting results with clinical information, and reporting safely.

Medical laboratory scientists, also called medical laboratory technologists or biomedical scientists in some countries, work in hospital and public health laboratories, research, industry and education. They combine scientific knowledge with careful technique, safety, ethics and communication.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Degrees have different names, including Bachelor of Medical Laboratory Science (BMLS), Bachelor of Science in Medical Laboratory Science or Medical Laboratory Technology, and biomedical science. Programmes usually begin with chemistry, physics, biology, mathematics, anatomy, physiology and terminology. Later years add laboratory disciplines, quality management, professional practice and research. Supervised practical training and a final project are common.

Length, award and internship rules differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, the usual award is the BMLS, and the Medical Laboratory Science Council of Nigeria (MLSCN) regulates the profession; check your handbook and MLSCN requirements. In the United Kingdom, biomedical science degrees are often three years, and accreditation and registration rules matter. In the United States, medical laboratory science is often a bachelor’s degree with certification routes. Confirm your own programme’s structure and licensure rules.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Most programmes start with profession and scope, laboratory safety, biosafety and biosecurity, terminology, units and laboratory mathematics, general and organic chemistry, physics and instrumentation, anatomy and physiology, cell biology and histology, foundations of microbiology, and specimen collection. These explain the normal body, laboratory hazards and principles behind later tests.

Core study covers clinical haematology, blood transfusion science and immunohaematology, clinical chemistry, clinical bacteriology, parasitology, mycology, diagnostic virology, immunology and serology, molecular diagnostics, histopathology and cytology, and clinical microscopy and body fluids. Alongside these come laboratory quality management and accreditation, laboratory management, informatics and health economics, diagnostic testing and test evaluation, public health laboratory practice and surveillance, professional practice, ethics and regulation, and research methods, biostatistics and scientific writing.

Master’s level work usually deepens research methods and biostatistics for a dissertation, advanced quality, accreditation and method validation, and molecular genomics and advanced diagnostics. Teaching order varies, but the logic is steady: normal science, then specimen and safety, then diagnostic disciplines, then quality, management, public health and research.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn normal structure and function before abnormal results. For each test, ask what it measures, which specimen is needed, when it is collected, what can interfere, and how the result is interpreted. Make short tables linking disease, specimen, test and expected change. Practise unit conversions and quality-control calculations until they are reliable.

Use the laboratory, not only books. Under supervision, watch specimen collection, processing, staining and instrument checks. Keep a logbook and write brief notes after each practical. Test yourself with past questions and explain results aloud. Space revision and revisit weak areas. Read current national or WHO guidance for public health topics, and follow local standard operating procedures.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
A common mistake is memorising test names and cut-off values without understanding the method or disease. Another is ignoring preanalytical errors: wrong container, wrong timing, delayed transport, haemolysed or clotted samples. These can change results more than the analyser does.

Some students treat reference intervals as universal. They vary with age, sex, pregnancy, method and population, so use the interval stated by your laboratory. Others confuse screening with diagnosis, or report a single result without quality control and clinical context.

Safety is another weak point: rushing, eating in the laboratory, poor hand hygiene, or incorrect waste disposal. Do not use notes like these to diagnose yourself or others. Laboratory results need qualified interpretation and current local guidance.

keyPoints: Medical laboratory science supports diagnosis, treatment, monitoring and public health through accurate laboratory testing.
The degree usually starts with basic sciences and safety, then moves to diagnostic disciplines, quality, management and research.
Degree names, length, internship and licensure differ by country, so check your own handbook and regulator.
Learn normal structure and function first, then link each test to specimen, method, interference and clinical meaning.
Preanalytical errors and poor quality control can change results more than the analyser does.
These notes teach concepts and are not medical advice; follow current national or WHO guidance and local protocols.

en.title: Medical laboratory science: the profession, its scope and career paths
en.short: The profession, its history, roles, laboratory sections, regulation and training pathways.

sections.heading: Origins and scope
sections.text:
Medical laboratory science is the health profession that performs and interprets tests on blood, urine, tissue and other specimens. It grew from nineteenth-century pathology, microbiology and chemistry, when staining, culture and chemical tests began to identify disease. It became a distinct profession in the twentieth century as hospitals set up diagnostic laboratories and training and regulation followed.

Its scope includes reliable results, quality, advice to clinicians and public health.

sections.heading: Roles in care
sections.text:
Laboratory results guide diagnosis, treatment monitoring and public health. Diagnosis identifies the cause of illness, for example malaria parasites in a blood film. Monitoring checks the response to treatment, for example a falling viral load in HIV care. Public health uses laboratory data to detect outbreaks, test water and food, and track antimicrobial resistance.

Case: a patient in a district hospital in Kenya has fever. A laboratory scientist performs malaria microscopy and a full blood count. The results help the team decide whether malaria is likely and whether other tests are needed. Confirmed cases are reported to local surveillance.

sections.heading: Main laboratory sections
sections.text: Main sections include clinical chemistry, haematology, microbiology (bacteriology, parasitology, mycology and virology), immunology and serology, histopathology and cytology, blood transfusion science, molecular diagnostics and public health laboratories. Careers span hospital, public health, research, industry and teaching laboratories.

sections.heading: Profession and regulation
sections.text:
Regulation protects the public by setting standards for entry, conduct and laboratory quality. Training pathways differ by country and may include diploma, bachelor’s and postgraduate programmes, supervised practice and registration. Professional bodies provide continuing education and advocacy.

For example, in Nigeria the Medical Laboratory Science Council of Nigeria (MLSCN) regulates the profession, and the Association of Medical Laboratory Scientists of Nigeria (AMLSN) is a professional association. In the United Kingdom, the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC) regulates biomedical scientists, and the Institute of Biomedical Science (IBMS) is the professional body. In the United States, clinical laboratories are regulated under CLIA. Check the current national regulator because rules change.

keyPoints: Medical laboratory science performs and interprets tests that support diagnosis, treatment monitoring and public health.
The profession grew from nineteenth-century pathology, microbiology and chemistry and became distinct in the twentieth century.
Main sections include clinical chemistry, haematology, microbiology, immunology, histopathology, blood transfusion, molecular diagnostics and public health.
Careers span hospital, public health, research, industry and teaching laboratories.
Regulation and training pathways differ by country; for example, MLSCN regulates in Nigeria and HCPC in the United Kingdom.
Always check the current national regulator and training requirements because rules change.

en.title: Laboratory safety, biosafety and biosecurity
en.short: Hazards, risk assessment, PPE, hand hygiene, sharps, spills, waste, biosafety levels and incident reporting.

sections.heading: Hazards and risk assessment
sections.text:
A hazard is anything that can cause harm; risk is the chance and severity of harm. Biological hazards include blood, cultures and aerosols. Chemical hazards include disinfectants and solvents; read the label and safety data sheet. Physical hazards include fire, electricity and slips. Ergonomic hazards include repetitive pipetting and poor posture.

Risk assessment identifies the hazard, who may be harmed, likelihood, severity and controls. Use the hierarchy: elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, then PPE. Review when work changes.

sections.heading: PPE and hand hygiene
sections.text:
Personal protective equipment (PPE) includes gloves, gown, mask, eye protection and closed shoes. Choose PPE for the task, put it on before work, and remove it without touching the outside. PPE does not replace other controls.

Hand hygiene is the most important routine measure. Wash with soap and water when hands are visibly dirty or after contact with spores; otherwise use alcohol-based hand rub. Clean hands before and after gloves, after blood contact, and after removing PPE.

sections.heading: Sharps, spills and waste
sections.text:
Never recap, bend or break needles. Place sharps immediately in a puncture-resistant, labelled container, and do not overfill it. For a biological spill, alert others, wear PPE, cover with absorbent, apply the laboratory disinfectant for the contact time in local policy, remove glass with forceps, clean and report.

Chemical spills need the safety data sheet and spill kit. Waste is segregated at source. Colour codes differ by country, so follow national and institutional rules.

sections.heading: Biosafety, biosecurity and reporting
sections.text:
Biosafety levels (BSL) rank containment. BSL-1 is low risk; BSL-2 covers most clinical laboratories; BSL-3 handles serious airborne agents; BSL-4 handles the most dangerous agents. Biosecurity protects pathogens from loss, theft and misuse through access control, inventory and secure storage.

Report incidents promptly: needlestick, splash, spill, broken container, missing sample or unauthorised access. Seek immediate assessment after exposure; post-exposure care follows national guidance. Case: Ada, a first-year student in Ibadan, drops a blood tube. She alerts her supervisor, puts on PPE, uses the spill kit and reports the incident.

keyPoints: A hazard is a source of harm; risk is the chance and severity of that harm.
Risk assessment follows the hierarchy of controls, and PPE is the last line of defence.
Hand hygiene is needed before and after gloves and after removing PPE.
Never recap needles; place sharps immediately in a puncture-resistant container.
BSL-2 covers most clinical laboratories; BSL-4 handles the most dangerous agents.
Report exposures and spills promptly, and follow current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Medical terminology, units and laboratory mathematics
en.short: Medical word parts, SI units, concentration, dilution and basic QC statistics for the laboratory.

sections.heading: Word parts and units
sections.text:
Medical terms are built from a prefix, root and suffix. The root gives the main meaning, the prefix changes it, and the suffix shows condition, process or study. For example, haematology: haemat- means blood and -logy means study.

SI units give one agreed system. Base units include metre, kilogram, second, mole, kelvin, ampere and candela. Volume: 1 L = 1 dm³ = 1000 mL, and 1 mL = 1 cm³. Mass: 1 g = 1000 mg = 1 000 000 micrograms. Amount: 1 mol = 1000 mmol.

Significant figures show measurement precision. Keep all digits during a calculation and round only at the end. For addition and subtraction, round to the least decimal places. For multiplication and division, round to the least significant figures.

sections.heading: Concentration and dilution
sections.text:
Mass concentration is mass of solute per volume of solution. Percentage weight/volume means grams per 100 mL: 5 g glucose in 100 mL is 50 g/L or 5% w/v. Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution. Moles = mass ÷ molar mass. For example, 0.585 g sodium chloride (molar mass 58.5 g/mol) in 100 mL: moles = 0.585 ÷ 58.5 = 0.0100 mol; molarity = 0.0100 ÷ 0.100 = 0.100 mol/L.

Dilution uses C1V1 = C2V2. To make 100 mL of 0.10 mol/L from 1.0 mol/L, V1 = (0.10 × 100) ÷ 1.0 = 10 mL; dilute 10 mL to 100 mL. Three 1 in 10 serial steps give 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000-fold dilution.

sections.heading: Quality-control statistics
sections.text:
Quality control checks precision and accuracy. Mean = Σx ÷ n. Standard deviation (SD) = √[Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)]. Coefficient of variation (CV) = (SD ÷ mean) × 100%.

For results 100, 102, 98 and 100 mg/dL: mean = 400 ÷ 4 = 100; SD = √(8 ÷ 3) = 1.63; CV = (1.63 ÷ 100) × 100 = 1.63%. Lower CV means better precision. Acceptable limits vary, so use the current local protocol or manufacturer’s instructions.

keyPoints: Medical terms are built from prefixes, roots and suffixes; learn each part and how it changes meaning.
Convert units by multiplying by powers of ten, and keep all digits until the final rounding.
Mass concentration = mass ÷ volume; molarity = moles ÷ litres, where moles = mass ÷ molar mass.
Dilution uses C1V1 = C2V2; serial dilutions multiply the dilution factors.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; SD = √[Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)]; CV = (SD ÷ mean) × 100%.
QC statistics describe precision, and acceptable limits must come from the current local protocol or manufacturer.

en.title: General, organic and biological chemistry
en.short: Atoms, bonding, solutions, pH, equilibria, organic groups and biomolecules.

sections.heading: Atoms and bonding
sections.text:
Atoms have protons and neutrons in the nucleus and electrons in shells. Atomic number is the proton count; mass number is protons plus neutrons. Isotopes differ in neutrons. Outer electrons determine bonding.

Ionic bonds transfer electrons and form ions held by electrostatic attraction, as in sodium chloride. Covalent bonds share electrons. Polar covalent bonds have unequal sharing, creating partial charges and hydrogen bonds, which stabilise water, proteins and DNA.

sections.heading: Solutions, pH and equilibria
sections.text:
Solutions contain a solute dissolved in a solvent. Concentration is amount per volume, often mol/L. Water self-ionises: H2O ⇌ H+ + OH−. pH is −log10[H+]. Strong acids dissociate fully; weak acids partly, described by Ka.

A buffer resists pH change when small acid or base amounts are added and works best near its pKa. Example: if [H+] = 1 × 10−4 mol/L, pH = −log10(10−4) = 4.0. Acetic acid with sodium acetate, pKa 4.76, buffers near pH 4.8. Equilibrium is reached when forward and reverse rates are equal; changing conditions shifts it.

sections.heading: Organic groups and biomolecules
sections.text:
Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds. Functional groups give properties: hydroxyl (−OH), carboxyl (−COOH), amino (−NH2), carbonyl (C=O) and phosphate. Reactions include oxidation, reduction, condensation and hydrolysis.

Carbohydrates are sugars and polymers such as starch and glycogen; glucose is a monosaccharide. Lipids include fats and steroids; triglycerides are glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds. Proteins are amino acid chains joined by peptide bonds; their shape depends on hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions. Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy; they are specific and depend on pH and temperature.

sections.heading: Metabolism outline
sections.text:
Metabolism is the chemical reactions in cells. Catabolism breaks molecules down and releases energy; anabolism builds molecules and uses energy. Glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate in the cytoplasm.

Aerobic respiration uses the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation to make ATP, energy currency. Fatty acids undergo beta-oxidation. Amino acids build proteins or are deaminated, with nitrogen excreted as urea. Enzymes control these pathways, so enzyme activity can indicate tissue damage.

keyPoints: Atomic number is the proton count, mass number is protons plus neutrons, and outer electrons determine bonding.
pH = −log10[H+], and buffers resist pH change, working best near their pKa; the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]).
At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, and changing concentration, pressure or temperature can shift the position.
Hydroxyl, carboxyl, amino, carbonyl and phosphate groups give organic molecules their chemical properties.
Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and enzymes are built by condensation and broken by hydrolysis, and enzymes lower activation energy.
Metabolism includes catabolism and anabolism; glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation produce ATP.

en.title: Physics and instrumentation for the laboratory
en.short: Measurement error, optics, spectrophotometry, centrifugation, electrophoresis, pH, temperature and electrical safety.

sections.heading: Measurement and error
sections.text:
Measurement compares a quantity with a standard. Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated results. Systematic error shifts every result the same way, often from poor calibration. Random error scatters results.

Pipetting 100 microlitres and getting 98, 99 and 99 microlitres shows bias (mean 98.7) plus scatter. Check instruments with standards and controls.

sections.heading: Optics and spectrophotometry
sections.text:
Spectrophotometry passes light of a chosen wavelength through a sample. Transmittance is the fraction of light reaching the detector; %T is that fraction as a percentage. Absorbance A = 2 − log10(%T). The Beer-Lambert law states A = ε × c × l, where ε is absorptivity, c concentration and l path length. With ε and l fixed, absorbance is proportional to concentration.

Worked example: %T = 50 gives A = 2 − 1.699 = 0.301. Colorimetry uses visible light and a coloured reaction; always use a blank and a calibration curve.

sections.heading: Centrifugation and electrophoresis
sections.text:
Centrifugation separates particles by density. Relative centrifugal force RCF = 1.118 × 10^−5 × r × rpm², with r the rotor radius in centimetres. For r = 10 cm at 3000 rpm: RCF = 1.118 × 10^−5 × 10 × 9,000,000 ≈ 1006 × g. Balance tubes and respect rotor limits.

Electrophoresis separates charged molecules in a gel under an electric field; movement depends on charge, size and shape.

sections.heading: pH, temperature and safety
sections.text:
pH ≈ −log10[H+] and is measured with a meter calibrated against standard buffers. Conductivity measures a solution’s ability to carry current, reflecting ion concentration; it is not pH. Temperature control relies on calibrated thermometers, incubators and water baths.

Electrical safety means earthing, fuses, residual current devices, dry hands and undamaged leads. Care for instruments by cleaning, calibrating, logging maintenance and following the manufacturer. Rules vary by country; check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated results.
Systematic error shifts all results one way; random error scatters them.
Absorbance A = 2 − log10(%T), and Beer-Lambert law A = ε × c × l.
RCF = 1.118 × 10^−5 × r × rpm², with r in centimetres.
pH ≈ −log10[H+]; conductivity measures ions, not pH.
Electrical safety needs earthing, fuses, residual current devices and dry hands.

en.title: Human anatomy and physiology for laboratory science
en.short: This summary covers organ systems, homeostasis, blood and body fluids, specimen sources and how physiology changes results.

sections.heading: Systems and homeostasis
sections.text:
Anatomy is structure; physiology is function. Major organ systems work together: the cardiovascular system moves blood, the respiratory system exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide, the renal system filters blood and balances water and electrolytes, the digestive system absorbs nutrients, and the endocrine and nervous systems coordinate responses.

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment around set points. Negative feedback corrects change: if blood glucose rises, insulin lowers it; if it falls, glucagon raises it. A specimen reflects a controlled system.

sections.heading: Blood and fluids
sections.text:
Blood is a fluid connective tissue. Plasma is the liquid part, containing water, electrolytes, proteins, glucose, hormones and waste. Erythrocytes carry oxygen, leukocytes defend the body, and platelets help clotting. Body fluids include intracellular and extracellular fluid, such as interstitial fluid, plasma, cerebrospinal fluid and urine. Water moves between compartments by osmosis.

In dehydration, plasma water falls, so haemoglobin and packed cell volume may rise even when red cell mass is unchanged.

sections.heading: Common specimens
sections.text:
Common specimens include venous blood, capillary blood, urine, stool, sputum, cerebrospinal fluid, swabs and tissue biopsy. Each has a source and composition. Venous blood is used for serum or plasma tests. Capillary blood suits small tests such as glucose. Urine forms when the kidneys filter plasma and then reabsorb most of the filtrate; it contains water, urea, creatinine, electrolytes and waste. Stool contains water, fibre, bacteria and cells.

Cerebrospinal fluid is normally clear, with much less protein and a lower glucose than plasma. A swab collects surface organisms; a biopsy samples tissue.

sections.heading: Results and variation
sections.text:
Physiological states change laboratory results. Age, sex, pregnancy, exercise, posture, diet, time of day and stress can shift values. Disease changes results by altering production, loss or metabolism. Amina has vomiting and diarrhoea. Dehydration concentrates her blood, so her haemoglobin and packed cell volume may rise, and her urine becomes concentrated. After fluids, values may return to baseline.

Reference intervals are the usual range for a healthy population. They depend on method and population, so use the laboratory’s own intervals and interpret with the clinical picture.

keyPoints: Anatomy is structure; physiology is function.
Homeostasis uses negative feedback to keep internal conditions near set points.
Blood plasma carries water, electrolytes, proteins, glucose, hormones and waste; cells and platelets have separate roles.
Common specimens differ in source and normal composition, so collection site matters.
Age, sex, pregnancy, exercise, posture, diet, time of day, stress and disease can change laboratory results.
Reference intervals depend on method and population; use the laboratory’s own intervals and the clinical picture.

en.title: Cell biology and basic histology
en.short: Cell structure, division, basic tissues, microscopy, and histological specimen preparation and staining.

sections.heading: Cell structure
sections.text:
A cell is the smallest living unit. The plasma membrane controls entry and exit. The nucleus holds DNA and directs activity. Mitochondria produce most ATP, the cell’s energy currency. Ribosomes make proteins. The rough endoplasmic reticulum folds and transports proteins; the smooth form makes lipids. The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages proteins. Lysosomes digest worn-out material. The cytoskeleton gives shape and movement.

Organelles cooperate: a secreted protein is made on ribosomes, processed in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi, then released in vesicles.

sections.heading: Division and tissues
sections.text:
Mitosis produces two genetically identical cells for growth and repair. Meiosis occurs in germ cells and produces gametes with half the chromosome number, creating variation. The cell cycle includes interphase, when DNA is copied, and mitosis.

Histology studies tissue structure. The four basic tissues are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous. Epithelium covers surfaces and lines cavities. Connective tissue supports and binds, including blood, bone and cartilage. Muscle contracts. Nervous tissue conducts impulses.

sections.heading: Microscopy
sections.text: A light microscope uses lenses to magnify. Total magnification is eyepiece magnification multiplied by objective magnification. With a 10× eyepiece and a 40× objective, total magnification is 10 × 40 = 400×. Resolution is the ability to see two close points as separate; it depends on wavelength and lens quality. Carry the microscope with two hands, start on low power, focus with the coarse knob only on low power, and use the fine knob at higher power.

sections.heading: Specimens and staining
sections.text:
Histological specimens need careful handling. Label the container, fix tissue promptly in adequate fixative, and avoid drying. Fixation preserves structure by cross-linking or precipitating proteins; buffered formalin is common. The specimen is dehydrated in graded alcohols, cleared, embedded in paraffin wax, sectioned with a microtome, stained and mounted.

Staining gives contrast. Haematoxylin stains nuclei blue-purple by binding acidic DNA. Eosin stains cytoplasm and collagen pink. This routine H&E stain needs controlled timing. Follow local safety rules for chemicals and sharps.

keyPoints: The plasma membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi and lysosomes have distinct roles.
Mitosis makes identical cells for growth and repair; meiosis makes gametes with half the chromosome number.
The four basic tissues are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous.
Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.
Fixation preserves tissue; haematoxylin stains nuclei and eosin stains cytoplasm.
Histological processing includes fixation, dehydration, clearing, embedding, sectioning, staining and mounting.

en.title: Foundations of medical microbiology
en.short: The main microorganism groups, growth, normal flora, sterilisation, culture, microscopy and infection control.

sections.heading: Groups of pathogens
sections.text:
Medical microbiology studies microorganisms that cause disease. Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes with no nucleus; they include cocci, bacilli and spirochaetes. Viruses are acellular and replicate only inside host cells. Fungi are eukaryotes, either yeasts or moulds. Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes, and helminths are multicellular worms. Prions are misfolded proteins, not microorganisms.

Size matters for diagnosis: most bacteria are seen with a light microscope after staining, while viruses need electron microscopy or molecular tests.

sections.heading: Growth and normal flora
sections.text:
Microbes grow by binary fission in bacteria or by other cycles in fungi and parasites. Growth needs nutrients, water, a suitable temperature and pH, and often a particular oxygen level.

Normal flora are organisms that live on skin and mucous membranes without causing disease. They compete with pathogens and aid digestion, but can cause infection if they enter sterile sites or if immunity falls. Colonisation means the organism is present without symptoms; infection means it causes damage.

sections.heading: Sterilisation and disinfection
sections.text:
Sterilisation destroys all microorganisms, including bacterial spores. Disinfection reduces the number of pathogens on inanimate objects but may not kill spores. Antisepsis is disinfection of living skin.

Methods include moist heat in an autoclave, dry heat, filtration, radiation and chemical agents. Spores resist many disinfectants, so choose a method suited to the item and follow the manufacturer’s instructions and national guidance.

sections.heading: Culture, microscopy and control
sections.text:
Culture means growing organisms on nutrient media. A specimen is inoculated, incubated and examined for colonies; Gram stain and biochemical tests help identify bacteria. Microscopy may use a wet mount or a stained smear.

Infection prevention and control rests on standard precautions: hand hygiene, protective clothing, safe sharps disposal and correct waste handling. Transmission-based precautions add isolation or masks for specific infections. Example: a wound swab from a patient in Kano grows Gram-positive cocci in clusters, suggesting Staphylococcus aureus; staff use standard precautions and clean equipment. WHO and national guidelines give current details.

keyPoints: Bacteria are prokaryotes; viruses need host cells; fungi, protozoa and helminths are eukaryotes.
Normal flora protect but can cause infection when displaced or immunity falls.
Sterilisation kills all microbes including spores; disinfection may not.
Culture and microscopy identify organisms by colony, stain and biochemical features.
Standard precautions are the basis of infection prevention and control.
Follow current WHO and national guidance for methods and precautions.

en.title: Specimen collection, handling and basic laboratory techniques
en.short: Covers specimen collection, labelling, transport, venepuncture, capillary sampling, pipetting, weighing, centrifugation.

sections.heading: Patient identification
sections.text: Before any sample, identify the patient with at least two independent identifiers, such as full name and hospital or clinic number. Ask the patient to state them; do not rely on a bed label alone. Check preparation: fasting, timing, medicines and consent, following the requesting clinician’s instructions and local policy. Venepuncture is restricted to staff trained and permitted under national and local rules; this varies by country.

sections.heading: Containers and labels
sections.text: Choose the container stated by the laboratory: sterile for microbiology, an additive tube, containing a chemical, for the test requested, or a plain tube for serum. Tube colours and additives differ between manufacturers and countries, so follow the local collection manual, not memory. Label at the bedside with patient identifiers, date and time, specimen type and collector. An unlabelled or mislabelled sample, wrong container, insufficient volume or delayed transport is usually rejected. Transport promptly in a leak-proof bag at the required temperature. Record collection and receipt.

sections.heading: Venepuncture and capillary
sections.text: Venepuncture means entering a vein with a needle to obtain blood. Capillary sampling uses a small skin prick, for example a finger or heel prick. Both require training, consent, aseptic technique (clean, contamination-free practice) and safe sharps disposal. Avoid prolonged tourniquet time and repeated probing. In capillary sampling, avoid excessive squeezing, which adds tissue fluid and dilutes the sample. Some tests need venous blood, not capillary blood. Follow local policy on who may collect and which site is allowed.

sections.heading: Basic techniques
sections.text: Pipetting measures liquid volume; read the meniscus (liquid surface) at eye level and use the correct pipette for the volume. Weighing uses a clean, calibrated balance, set to zero with its container. Centrifugation separates parts by density; balance tubes by weight opposite each other. Relative centrifugal force (RCF) depends on rotor radius and speed: RCF = 1.118 × 0.00001 × radius in cm × rpm². For radius 10 cm at 3,000 rpm, RCF ≈ 1,006 × g. Handle glassware carefully and document every step.

keyPoints: Use at least two independent identifiers before collecting any specimen.
Label specimens at the bedside with patient details, time, type and collector.
Follow local rejection criteria; unlabelled, mislabelled, wrong-container or delayed samples are usually rejected.
Venepuncture and capillary sampling require training, consent, aseptic technique and local permission.
Read the meniscus at eye level and use a calibrated balance set to zero.
RCF = 1.118 × 0.00001 × radius in cm × rpm²; check tube balancing before centrifugation.

en.title: Clinical haematology: blood cells and laboratory diagnosis
en.short: Blood cell formation, FBC interpretation, anaemias, haemoglobinopathies, haemostasis and laboratory QC.

sections.heading: Blood cell formation
sections.text: Haematopoiesis is the formation of blood cells in bone marrow from haematopoietic stem cells. Erythropoietin drives red cell production, G-CSF drives granulocyte production, and thrombopoietin drives platelet production. Morphology is studied on a stained blood film, usually Wright, Leishman or Giemsa stain. Assess red cell size, colour and shape, and white cell nucleus, cytoplasm and granules. Terms include microcytic and macrocytic for size, hypochromic for pale cells, poikilocytosis for shape variation, and anisocytosis for size variation.

sections.heading: Full blood count
sections.text: The full blood count measures haemoglobin, red cell count, haematocrit (packed cell volume, PCV), red cell indices, white cell count with differential, and platelet count. Automated analysers flag abnormal results, and a blood film is reviewed when needed. Red cell indices are calculated: MCV = Hct ÷ RBC; MCH = Hb ÷ RBC; MCHC = Hb ÷ Hct. Example: Hb 7.5 g/dL, RBC 4.0×10^12/L, Hct 0.24 L/L. MCV = 0.24 ÷ 4.0 = 0.060×10^−12 L = 60 fL. MCH = 75 g/L ÷ 4.0×10^12/L = 18.75 pg. MCHC = 7.5 ÷ 0.24 = 31.25 g/dL. This suggests microcytic hypochromic anaemia. Reference intervals vary with age, sex, altitude and analyser; use local ranges.

sections.heading: Anaemias and haemoglobinopathies
sections.text: Anaemia is a haemoglobin level below the reference interval for age and sex. Classify by MCV: microcytic anaemia includes iron deficiency and thalassaemia; normocytic anaemia includes blood loss, chronic disease and haemolysis; macrocytic anaemia includes vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, liver disease and alcohol. The reticulocyte count shows the marrow response. Haemoglobinopathies include sickle cell disease and the thalassaemias. Confirm with haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC, and use genetic testing where available.

sections.heading: White cells, platelets, haemostasis and QC
sections.text: White cell disorders include neutropenia, neutrophilia, lymphocytosis and leukaemia. Platelet disorders include thrombocytopenia, thrombocytosis and platelet function defects. Basic haemostasis tests are platelet count, PT/INR, APTT, fibrinogen and D-dimer; interpret them with the clinical history. Haematology quality control includes analyser calibration, daily internal QC, review of Levey-Jennings charts, external quality assessment, delta checks and blood film review.

keyPoints: Haematopoiesis occurs in bone marrow under growth factors such as erythropoietin, G-CSF and thrombopoietin.
The full blood count includes Hb, RBC, Hct, indices, white cell differential and platelets; review the film when flags appear.
MCV = Hct ÷ RBC, MCH = Hb ÷ RBC, and MCHC = Hb ÷ Hct; convert to consistent units before calculating.
Anaemia is classified by MCV as microcytic, normocytic or macrocytic; the reticulocyte count shows marrow response.
Haemoglobinopathies are confirmed by haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC, not by a single screening test alone.
Haematology QC uses calibration, daily internal QC, external quality assessment and delta checks.

en.title: Blood transfusion science and immunohaematology
en.short: ABO and RhD groups, antibody screening, crossmatching, components, reactions, haemovigilance and donor safety.

sections.heading: Groups and compatibility
sections.text:
Blood groups are inherited red-cell antigens. In ABO, group A has A antigen and anti-B antibody; group B has B antigen and anti-A; group AB has both antigens and no antibodies; group O has neither and both antibodies. These IgM antibodies can cause immediate haemolysis. RhD-positive cells carry D antigen; RhD-negative people may form IgG anti-D after exposure, which can cross the placenta.

Donor antigens must not meet matching recipient antibodies. Group O RhD-negative red cells are often called universal donor cells, but local rules apply. Case: a group A patient given group B red cells has anti-B that attacks donor cells, causing fever, loin pain and haemoglobinuria. Stop the transfusion and report it.

sections.heading: Screening and crossmatching
sections.text: Antibody screening detects unexpected antibodies in patient serum. The indirect antiglobulin test (IAT) mixes serum with reagent red cells, then adds antihuman globulin to show bound IgG. A positive screen needs antibody identification. Crossmatching tests donor red cells against patient serum. It confirms ABO compatibility and, with IAT, checks for clinically significant antibodies. Electronic crossmatch is allowed only under strict criteria. Follow current national protocols.

sections.heading: Components and storage
sections.text: Blood is separated into components. Red cells are stored at 2 to 6 °C; platelets at 20 to 24 °C with gentle agitation; plasma is frozen, commonly at -25 °C or colder. Shelf lives and temperatures vary by country and anticoagulant, so check national blood service guidance. Labels must show component, group, donation and expiry dates.

sections.heading: Reactions and safety
sections.text: Transfusion reactions include acute haemolytic, febrile non-haemolytic, allergic, anaphylactic, septic, transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) and circulatory overload (TACO). Stop the transfusion, keep the line open with saline, and report. Haemovigilance is the national system for recording and learning from adverse events and near misses. Donor selection uses a health questionnaire, haemoglobin check and screening for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis; malaria screening is added where relevant. Blood safety depends on voluntary non-remunerated donors, accurate testing, quality systems and WHO or national guidance.

keyPoints: ABO antibodies are usually IgM and cause immediate haemolysis; RhD anti-D is IgG and can cross the placenta.
Antibody screening uses the indirect antiglobulin test; crossmatching confirms ABO and clinically significant antibody compatibility.
Red cells are stored at 2 to 6 °C, platelets at 20 to 24 °C with agitation, and plasma frozen; check national guidance for shelf life.
Acute haemolytic reaction after ABO-incompatible red cells presents with fever, loin pain and haemoglobinuria; stop and report.
Haemovigilance records adverse events and near misses to improve transfusion safety.
Donor selection and blood safety rely on questionnaires, infection screening, voluntary non-remunerated donors and quality systems.

en.title: Clinical chemistry and organ-function testing
en.short: Analytes, electrolytes, acid-base, renal, liver, cardiac and thyroid tests, interferences and quality control.

sections.heading: Analytes and reference intervals
sections.text: An analyte is the substance being measured, such as sodium, glucose or creatinine. A reference interval is the range that contains 95% of results from a healthy reference population, so about 5% of healthy people fall outside it. Intervals are method and population specific, so use the interval printed by your own laboratory, not a textbook value. Results are compared with the interval and with the patient’s previous results.

sections.heading: Electrolytes and acid-base
sections.text: Sodium, potassium, chloride and bicarbonate are the main electrolytes. The anion gap helps classify metabolic acidosis: sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate). For example, 140 − (104 + 24) = 12 mmol/L. Many laboratories use a reference interval of about 8 to 16 mmol/L, but each laboratory sets its own. Blood gas analysis measures pH, pCO2 and bicarbonate. A low pH with low bicarbonate suggests metabolic acidosis; a low pH with high pCO2 suggests respiratory acidosis. Compensation is partial or complete, and mixed disorders occur.

sections.heading: Renal, liver, cardiac, thyroid
sections.text: Renal function tests include creatinine, urea and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Creatinine rises late in kidney disease, so eGFR is preferred for staging. Liver tests include bilirubin, albumin, and enzymes such as alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT). ALT is fairly liver specific; ALP rises in cholestasis and bone disease. Cardiac troponin is the preferred marker of myocardial injury; natriuretic peptides help assess heart failure. Thyroid tests usually start with thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), with free thyroxine (FT4) added when TSH is abnormal.

sections.heading: Quality control and interference
sections.text: Internal quality control runs control materials with known values alongside patient samples and plots results on Levey-Jennings charts; Westgard rules flag random and systematic error. External quality assessment compares your laboratory with others. Interference is anything that changes the measured result without changing the true concentration. Common examples are haemolysis, lipaemia and icterus, often screened by the HIL index, and drugs or contamination. Haemolysis falsely raises potassium and lactate dehydrogenase. Check a surprising result before reporting it.

keyPoints: Reference intervals are laboratory-specific and cover the central 95% of healthy results.
Anion gap = sodium − (chloride + bicarbonate); a typical interval is about 8 to 16 mmol/L but each laboratory sets its own.
Blood gas pH, pCO2 and bicarbonate separate metabolic from respiratory acid-base disorders.
Creatinine and eGFR assess renal function; bilirubin, albumin, ALT, AST, ALP and GGT assess liver function.
Cardiac troponin marks myocardial injury, and thyroid testing usually starts with TSH, with free T4 added when TSH is abnormal.
Internal QC with Levey-Jennings charts and Westgard rules, plus external assessment, detects error; haemolysis, lipaemia and icterus interfere.

en.title: Clinical bacteriology
en.short: Specimen processing, culture media, staining, identification, susceptibility testing, reporting and quality control.

sections.heading: Specimens and culture
sections.text: Clinical bacteriology turns a properly collected specimen into a clinically useful result. Specimens must come from the infection site, be taken before antibiotics when possible, and reach the laboratory in the correct container and transport medium. The laboratory records the specimen, examines it directly, and inoculates culture media. General-purpose media grow many organisms; selective media suppress unwanted ones; differential media show colour changes from specific reactions; enrichment media increase small numbers. Incubation temperature, atmosphere and time depend on the suspected organism. A culture is read by colony appearance, and pure growth is subcultured for identification.

sections.heading: Stains and identification
sections.text: Stains give a first clue. Gram stain uses crystal violet, iodine, alcohol and a counterstain: Gram-positive bacteria retain purple, Gram-negative bacteria appear pink or red. Ziehl-Neelsen stain detects acid-fast bacilli such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Biochemical tests identify organisms by their enzymes and metabolism, for example catalase, coagulase, oxidase, urease and sugar fermentation. Immunological tests use antibodies to detect bacterial antigens or identify isolates, such as latex agglutination. Results are interpreted together, not from one test alone.

sections.heading: Susceptibility testing
sections.text: Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) predicts whether an antibiotic is likely to work. Disk diffusion places antibiotic-impregnated disks on a lawn of bacteria; the zone of inhibition is measured. Dilution methods find the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), the lowest concentration that stops visible growth. Results are interpreted using current breakpoints from standards such as CLSI or EUCAST, which differ by country and are updated. AST must follow a standard method, because inoculum density, medium and incubation affect results.

sections.heading: Reporting and quality
sections.text: Reports give the organism, the specimen, and susceptibility as susceptible, intermediate or resistant, with comments when needed. Critical results are communicated promptly. Quality control protects reliability: media are tested for sterility and growth support, reference strains check each run, and external quality assessment compares the laboratory with others. Laboratories follow current national guidance and WHO recommendations, which change, so always check the latest official source.

keyPoints: Collect specimens from the infection site before antibiotics when possible, and use correct transport media.
General, selective, differential and enrichment media serve different culture purposes.
Gram stain separates Gram-positive (purple) from Gram-negative (pink or red) bacteria; Ziehl-Neelsen detects acid-fast bacilli.
Biochemical and immunological tests identify isolates and must be interpreted together.
Disk diffusion measures inhibition zones; dilution methods give the MIC, interpreted with current CLSI or EUCAST breakpoints.
Report organism and susceptibility clearly, communicate critical results, and run internal and external quality control.

en.title: Medical parasitology
en.short: Protozoa, helminths, life cycles, stool, urine and blood diagnosis, malaria tests and quality control.

sections.heading: Parasites and life cycles
sections.text:
A parasite lives in or on a host. Protozoa are single-celled parasites; helminths are worms. Important protozoa include Plasmodium, Entamoeba, Giardia and Trypanosoma. Important helminths include Schistosoma, Ascaris, hookworm and Wuchereria. A definitive host carries the sexual stage; an intermediate host carries a larval or asexual stage; a vector transmits infection. Humans may be definitive, intermediate or accidental hosts.

In schistosomiasis, eggs leave in stool or urine, miracidia (larvae) infect snails, and cercariae (larvae) penetrate skin. The cycle explains which specimen to examine.

sections.heading: Specimen examination
sections.text:
Stool examination looks for eggs, cysts (resting forms) and trophozoites (active forms). Direct wet mounts are quick; concentration methods such as formol-ether recover more parasites. Urine examination is used for Schistosoma haematobium eggs and sometimes microfilariae (filarial larvae). Blood films detect malaria parasites, trypanosomes and microfilariae. Stool and urine should be fresh, or preserved if delay is unavoidable.

Case: Amina, a 7-year-old in Kano with chronic diarrhoea, has Giardia cysts in stool; a stool antigen test is positive. The laboratory reports what it sees and the clinician correlates.

sections.heading: Malaria and blood parasites
sections.text:
Malaria diagnosis uses thick films for detection and thin films for species identification, stained with Giemsa. Microscopy shows the parasite and its stage. Rapid diagnostic tests detect parasite antigens, commonly Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein 2 or parasite lactate dehydrogenase; they help where microscopy is limited, but they cannot show parasite density or stage. Molecular tests are sensitive and help with species and mixed infections.

Other blood parasites include trypanosomes and microfilariae. Follow current WHO and national malaria guidance for testing and confirmation.

sections.heading: Quality control
sections.text:
Quality control protects accuracy. Use trained microscopists, correctly stored reagents and standard stains. Include known positive and negative slides, check stain batches, and re-read a sample of slides blindly. Record results clearly, including species and stage.

Antigen and molecular tests need kit controls, temperature control and measures against contamination. External quality assessment compares your results with other laboratories. Repeat unexpected results and review the specimen and request.

keyPoints: Protozoa are single-celled parasites; helminths are worms, and life cycles guide specimen choice.
Stool microscopy looks for eggs, cysts and trophozoites; concentration improves recovery.
Urine is examined for Schistosoma haematobium eggs; blood films for malaria, trypanosomes and microfilariae.
Thick films detect malaria, thin films identify species, and antigen or molecular tests support diagnosis under current guidance.
Quality control includes trained staff, standard stains, known controls, blind re-reading and external assessment.
Report species and stage, and repeat unexpected results.

en.title: Medical mycology
en.short: Fungal infections, specimen collection, microscopy, culture, susceptibility testing and laboratory safety.

sections.heading: Infection groups
sections.text: Medical mycology studies fungal infections, called mycoses. Superficial mycoses affect skin, hair, nails or outer surfaces, such as dermatophyte tinea and Malassezia. Subcutaneous mycoses enter through broken skin and spread locally, as in sporotrichosis and mycetoma. Systemic mycoses affect deep organs or blood, especially in immunocompromised people; examples include Candida, Cryptococcus, Aspergillus and dimorphic endemic fungi. Dimorphic means mould in the environment and yeast in tissue. Case: a farmer with painless foot nodules after thorn injury needs fungal as well as bacterial culture, because mycetoma can be either.

sections.heading: Specimens and microscopy
sections.text: Collect from the active site before antifungal treatment when possible. Send skin scales, nail clippings and plucked hairs for superficial disease; pus, aspirate or biopsy for subcutaneous disease; blood, cerebrospinal fluid, respiratory samples or tissue for systemic disease. Label, transport promptly and prevent drying. Direct microscopy is rapid. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) dissolves keratin and shows hyphae or spores in skin and nails. Calcofluor white binds fungal cell walls and is seen with a fluorescence microscope. Tissue may need periodic acid-Schiff or silver stains. India ink can show the Cryptococcus capsule in cerebrospinal fluid.

sections.heading: Culture and identification
sections.text: Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar, often with antibiotics, allows colony study. Incubate at suitable temperatures; some fungi grow at 25 to 30 degrees Celsius and some need 37 degrees Celsius. Identify by colony appearance, microscopic morphology in lactophenol cotton blue, germ tube test for Candida albicans, biochemical tests or molecular methods. Do not identify a mould from colony colour alone. Culture may take days to weeks, so early negative results do not exclude infection.

sections.heading: Susceptibility and safety
sections.text: Antifungal susceptibility testing estimates response. Broth dilution gives the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), the lowest drug concentration that visibly inhibits growth; disk diffusion measures zones. Interpret with current species-specific breakpoints from CLSI or EUCAST, because methods and breakpoints change. Testing is not routine for every fungus. For safety, mould cultures release spores: work in a biosafety cabinet, seal plates, wear protective clothing, decontaminate surfaces and autoclave waste. Follow national biosafety classification; dimorphic pathogens may need higher containment.

keyPoints: Superficial mycoses involve skin, hair and nails; subcutaneous mycoses spread locally; systemic mycoses affect deep organs, often in immunocompromised people.
Collect specimens from the active site before treatment and transport the correct sample type promptly.
KOH microscopy is rapid; culture on Sabouraud agar and microscopic morphology support identification.
Culture can take days to weeks, so early negative results do not exclude fungal infection.
Antifungal susceptibility uses MIC or zone size with current species-specific breakpoints; not every fungus needs testing.
Mould cultures release spores, so use a biosafety cabinet, sealed plates and national biosafety precautions.

en.title: Diagnostic virology
en.short: Virus structure, specimens, culture, antigen, serology, molecular tests, viral load, biosafety and quality control.

sections.heading: Virus basics
sections.text: Viruses are small infectious agents with a nucleic acid genome, either DNA or RNA, inside a protein capsid. Some have a lipid envelope. They cannot replicate alone, so they enter a host cell and use its machinery. Replication runs through attachment, entry, uncoating, genome copying and protein synthesis, assembly, and release. Enveloped viruses are fragile, so handling matters.

sections.heading: Specimens and transport
sections.text: Collect the right specimen from the right site at the right time. Respiratory infections need nasopharyngeal or throat swabs; systemic infection may need blood or cerebrospinal fluid; skin lesions need vesicle fluid or swabs; gastrointestinal infection needs stool. Put swabs in viral transport medium, keep samples cold, and avoid repeated freeze-thaw. Label fully and send promptly. Poor collection or delay causes false-negative results.

sections.heading: Detection methods
sections.text: Cell culture uses living cells and detects cytopathic effect (visible virus-induced cell damage), but it is slow and needs skilled staff. Antigen tests, such as immunofluorescence and enzyme immunoassay, are faster but less sensitive than molecular tests. Serology detects IgM and IgG antibodies; it helps with past or recent infection but has a window period (the delay before antibodies become detectable) and cross-reactivity. Molecular methods, mainly PCR (polymerase chain reaction) and RT-PCR (reverse-transcription PCR), detect viral nucleic acid and are highly sensitive. They need good extraction, controls and contamination control.

sections.heading: Viral load, safety and quality
sections.text: Viral load testing measures the amount of virus, usually as copies/mL or IU/mL (international units), and monitors HIV, hepatitis B and cytomegalovirus. Changes are often expressed on a log10 scale. For example, a fall from 100,000 to 1,000 copies/mL is a 2 log10 reduction, because 100,000 is 10^5 and 1,000 is 10^3. Use the same assay for monitoring. Work at the containment level required for the virus, often biosafety level 2 (BSL-2) for routine specimens and BSL-3 for high-risk work. Include positive and negative controls, validate assays, and join proficiency testing. Check current WHO or national guidance for clinical thresholds.

keyPoints: Viruses need a host cell to replicate and are classified by genome and envelope.
Collect the correct specimen early, use viral transport medium, keep it cold and avoid freeze-thaw.
Molecular tests are generally more sensitive than antigen tests or cell culture.
Serology detects antibodies and has a window period and cross-reactivity.
Viral load is reported in copies/mL or IU/mL, and changes are expressed as log10 reductions; log10 reduction = log10(starting load) − log10(ending load).
Use the required biosafety level, controls, validation and proficiency testing, and check current WHO or national guidance for clinical thresholds.

en.title: Immunology and serology
en.short: Innate and adaptive immunity, antibodies, ELISA, serological diagnosis and result interpretation.

sections.heading: Innate and adaptive immunity
sections.text: Innate immunity is the first line: physical barriers, phagocytes, natural killer cells, complement and inflammation. It acts within hours, has no memory and recognises broad patterns. Adaptive immunity is slower, specific and remembers. B lymphocytes make antibodies (humoral immunity); T lymphocytes kill infected cells or help other cells (cell-mediated immunity). A second exposure gives a faster, stronger secondary response. Vaccination uses this principle.

sections.heading: Antigens and antibodies
sections.text: An antigen is any substance that the immune system recognises. An epitope is the small part an antibody binds. Antibodies are immunoglobulins: IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE and IgD. IgM appears first in infection; IgG appears later and can cross the placenta. Complement is a group of plasma proteins that help kill microbes and clear immune complexes. It can also damage host cells.

sections.heading: Hypersensitivity and autoimmunity
sections.text: Hypersensitivity is harmful immune reaction. Type I is immediate allergy (IgE). Type II is antibody against fixed antigens, as in some drug reactions. Type III is immune-complex disease, as in serum sickness. Type IV is delayed, T-cell mediated, as in contact dermatitis. Autoimmunity is immune attack on self. Examples include rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes. Serology can show autoantibodies, but results must fit the clinical picture.

sections.heading: ELISA and serology
sections.text: ELISA is a common immunoassay: antigen or antibody is bound to a plate, then detected with an enzyme and substrate that change colour. Formats include direct, indirect, sandwich and competitive. Rapid tests, agglutination and chemiluminescence are also used. Serology detects antibody or antigen in serum. Paired acute and convalescent samples can show a rising titre. A titre is the highest dilution that still gives a positive result: if serum is positive at 1:80 but negative at 1:160, the titre is 80. Quality control matters: controls must be in range or the run is invalid. Interpret with the kit insert, cut-off, cross-reactions, the window period (the time between infection and when a test turns positive) and clinical context. National or WHO guidance should be followed for diagnosis.

keyPoints: Innate immunity is fast and non-specific; adaptive immunity is specific and has memory.
IgM appears early in infection; IgG appears later and crosses the placenta.
Hypersensitivity types I to IV are IgE allergy, antibody-mediated, immune-complex and delayed T-cell reactions.
ELISA detects antigen or antibody using an enzyme-linked colour change; controls must pass before results are accepted.
A titre is the highest dilution that still gives a positive result.
Serology must be interpreted with the kit cut-off, cross-reactions, window period and clinical findings.

en.title: Molecular diagnostics
en.short: Nucleic acid extraction, PCR, real-time PCR, sequencing, contamination control, quality and clinical use.

sections.heading: Extraction and PCR
sections.text:
Molecular diagnostics detects specific DNA or RNA sequences. Nucleic acid extraction starts with lysis, which breaks cells or viruses open. Proteins and inhibitors are removed, and nucleic acids are captured on silica or magnetic beads, washed, then eluted in buffer. Poor extraction causes false negatives, so lysis and inhibition controls matter.

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) copies a target sequence. Each cycle has denaturation, primer annealing and extension by a thermostable DNA polymerase. Primers define the target. Repeated cycles double the product, so 30 cycles can make about 2^30, over one billion copies, from one template. Real-time PCR measures fluorescence each cycle; the cycle threshold (Ct or Cq) falls as target amount rises, allowing quantification.

sections.heading: Sequencing and control
sections.text:
Sequencing reads the order of bases. Sanger sequencing uses chain-terminating nucleotides and capillary electrophoresis for single targets. Next-generation sequencing reads millions of fragments in parallel, useful for variants, resistance mutations and outbreak genomes. Results need bioinformatic interpretation.

Contamination is a major risk because amplified products are abundant. Use unidirectional workflow: reagent preparation, extraction and amplification in separate areas; aliquot reagents; use filter tips; include negative controls; clean surfaces. Uracil-N-glycosylase can prevent carry-over in some assays.

sections.heading: Quality and limits
sections.text:
Quality assurance covers the whole pathway: validated methods, standard operating procedures, trained staff, equipment calibration, internal controls and external quality assessment. Positive and negative controls must behave as expected. Laboratories should participate in proficiency testing and investigate failures. Guidelines and accreditation requirements differ by country; follow current national rules and WHO guidance.

Molecular tests are fast and sensitive, and can detect pathogens, resistance genes, inherited variants and cancer markers. Limitations include false negatives from inhibitors or low target, false positives from contamination, inability to tell live from dead organisms, and detection of variants of uncertain significance. Cost, power supply, cold chain and expert interpretation can restrict use. A molecular result must be interpreted with the clinical picture and, where relevant, confirmed by another method.

keyPoints: Nucleic acid extraction must remove inhibitors and be controlled to avoid false negatives.
PCR uses denaturation, annealing and extension; after n cycles, copies ≈ starting copies × 2^n.
Real-time PCR quantifies target from fluorescence, and a lower Ct means more target.
Separate pre- and post-amplification areas, aliquot reagents and run negative controls to control contamination.
Quality assurance includes validation, SOPs, controls, calibration, competency and external quality assessment.
Molecular tests are sensitive but can give false results and must be interpreted with clinical and local guidance.

en.title: Histopathology and cytology
en.short: Covers tissue fixation, processing, staining, cytology, frozen sections, microscopy, reporting and safety.

sections.heading: Fixation and processing
sections.text: Histopathology examines tissue to diagnose disease. Fixation preserves tissue by stopping autolysis (self-digestion) and hardening it. The routine fixative is 10% neutral buffered formalin; the volume and time depend on specimen size and local protocol. Processing removes water through graded alcohols, clears with a solvent such as xylene, and infiltrates with melted paraffin. Embedding places tissue in a paraffin block, correctly oriented. A microtome cuts thin sections, usually a few micrometres thick, which are mounted on slides.

sections.heading: Stains and frozen sections
sections.text: Routine staining is haematoxylin and eosin (H&E): haematoxylin stains nuclei blue and eosin stains cytoplasm and collagen pink. Special stains answer specific questions, such as periodic acid-Schiff for glycogen or fungi, Ziehl-Neelsen for acid-fast bacilli, and silver stains for reticulin. Immunohistochemistry uses antibodies to detect proteins and helps identify tumour type. Frozen sections are cut in a cryostat, a refrigerated microtome, from fresh tissue during surgery. They are rapid but less precise than paraffin sections, so they guide immediate decisions and are confirmed later.

sections.heading: Cytology
sections.text: Cytology studies individual cells rather than whole tissue architecture. Exfoliative samples, cells shed from surfaces, include cervical smears, sputum and urine. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) samples a lump with a thin needle. Cells may be smeared, fixed in alcohol or air-dried, then stained, for example by Papanicolaou or Giemsa methods. Cytology can screen, triage or diagnose, but it may need histology confirmation. Reporting uses standard systems that differ by country and site; check current national guidance.

sections.heading: Reporting and safety
sections.text: Microscopy reporting describes the specimen, gross appearance, microscopic findings and diagnosis, with comments on limitations. Quality control includes correct labelling, validated stains, positive and negative controls, equipment maintenance, review of discrepancies and retained records. Safety requires trained staff, good ventilation, personal protective equipment, spill kits and safe waste disposal. Formalin is toxic and a carcinogen; xylene is flammable. For example, a breast lump FNAC reported as suspicious should be confirmed by histology before treatment. This is education, not medical advice.

keyPoints: Fixation in 10% neutral buffered formalin preserves tissue; processing dehydrates, clears and infiltrates with paraffin.
H&E is the routine stain; special stains and immunohistochemistry answer specific diagnostic questions.
Cytology examines individual cells; FNAC and exfoliative samples may need histology confirmation.
Frozen sections are rapid intraoperative sections from fresh tissue and are less precise than paraffin sections.
Reports should describe the specimen, findings and diagnosis, and state limitations.
Quality control includes controls, maintenance and discrepancy review; formalin and xylene require ventilation and protective equipment.

en.title: Clinical microscopy and body-fluid analysis
en.short: Urine, CSF, pleural, peritoneal and synovial fluid, semen: microscopy, counts, crystals and quality control.

sections.heading: Urinalysis
sections.text: A reagent strip (dipstick) has pads that change colour for glucose, protein, blood, leucocyte esterase, nitrite and pH. Read each pad at the maker’s stated time; late reading causes false results. Check expiry, storage and controls. Microscopy examines centrifuged sediment and reports red cells, white cells, epithelial cells, casts and crystals. A cast is a cylindrical mould of a renal tubule. Crystals vary with urine pH and may be normal or pathological. Use a counting chamber for cell counts and a calibrated microscope.

sections.heading: Body fluids
sections.text: CSF, pleural, peritoneal and synovial fluids are counted in a haemocytometer and differentiated after spinning cells onto a slide. CSF is usually clear and low in cells; a traumatic tap adds blood. Pleural fluid is classified as exudate or transudate using protein and lactate dehydrogenase compared with serum (Light’s criteria). Peritoneal fluid is usually classified with the serum-ascites albumin gradient. Synovial fluid is examined for cells and crystals under polarised light: monosodium urate needles are negatively birefringent, calcium pyrophosphate rhomboids positively birefringent. Compare with serum and clinical findings.

sections.heading: Semen and counts
sections.text: Semen analysis follows the current WHO laboratory manual: volume, pH, liquefaction, concentration, motility and morphology. Use current manual and local limits; reference limits change by edition and laboratory. In an improved Neubauer chamber, each large square is 1 mm² and 0.1 mm deep, so its volume is 0.1 µL. Cells/µL = (count × dilution × 10) ÷ large squares counted. Example: 20 cells in four squares, no dilution: 20 × 1 × 10 ÷ 4 = 50 cells/µL. Check the arithmetic and chamber depth.

sections.heading: Interpretation and QC
sections.text: Interpret results with reference intervals, clinical history and previous samples. Quality control includes strip and control checks, chamber calibration, duplicate counts, stain quality and documented maintenance. Report specimen type, appearance, counts, differential and crystals. Critical results need urgent local reporting. Guidelines and reference values differ by country and change; follow current national or WHO guidance. These tests support diagnosis and are not medical advice.

keyPoints: Reagent strips must be read at the stated time and checked with controls.
Urine microscopy reports cells, casts and crystals; casts are renal tubule moulds.
Body fluids need cell counts, differentials and comparison with serum.
Synovial crystals are identified by shape and birefringence under polarised light.
Semen analysis follows the current WHO manual and local reference limits.
Cells/µL = (count × dilution × 10) ÷ large squares counted for a 0.1 mm deep chamber.

en.title: Laboratory quality management and accreditation
en.short: QC, QA, errors, SOPs, audits, EQA, method validation and ISO 15189 accreditation.

sections.heading: Quality control and assurance
sections.text:
Quality control (QC) checks each analytical run. You test control materials with known target values and compare the results with acceptable limits. Quality assurance (QA) is wider: it covers every phase, including procedures, training, equipment, audits and corrective action. Continuous improvement uses cycles such as Plan-Do-Check-Act and corrective and preventive action (CAPA) to fix causes, not just mistakes.

A simple QC example: a control has mean 100 and standard deviation (SD) 2. A result of 105 gives z = (105 − 100) ÷ 2 = 2.5. This lies outside ±2SD, so pause and investigate before reporting patient results.

sections.heading: Errors and SOPs
sections.text:
Preanalytical errors happen before testing: wrong patient identification, poor collection, delayed transport or wrong storage. Analytical errors happen during testing: calibration drift, expired reagents, instrument faults or failed QC. Postanalytical errors happen after testing: transcription mistakes, wrong reference ranges or delayed reports. Many errors begin before analysis, so collection and labelling deserve close attention.

A standard operating procedure (SOP) is a written, approved instruction for a task. Audits are systematic checks that practice follows the SOP and the quality system. A case: a clinic labels a sample with the wrong name; the laboratory rejects it and requests a repeat. That is a preanalytical error caught by a good SOP.

sections.heading: EQA, validation and accreditation
sections.text:
External quality assessment (EQA), or proficiency testing, sends unknown samples to many laboratories and compares their results. It reveals problems that internal QC may miss. Method validation is the formal check, before routine use, that a method is fit for purpose: precision, trueness, linearity and interference are examined.

ISO 15189 is the international standard for medical laboratories, covering quality and competence. Accreditation is independent assessment against that standard by an accreditation body. It is periodic, not a one-time certificate. Arrangements differ by country, so check your national accreditation body and current ISO guidance.

keyPoints: QC tests control materials with each run; QA covers the whole pathway.
Preanalytical, analytical and postanalytical errors can all harm patients; many begin before analysis.
An SOP is a written, approved instruction for a task.
Audits check practice against the SOP; EQA compares results with other laboratories.
Method validation confirms fitness for purpose before routine use.
For QC, z = (result − mean) ÷ SD; ISO 15189 accreditation is independent, periodic recognition of quality and competence.

en.title: Laboratory management, informatics and health economics
en.short: How laboratories are organised, supplied, scheduled, budgeted and linked to clinicians by information systems.

sections.heading: Organisation and staffing
sections.text: A laboratory is organised into sections such as haematology, clinical chemistry, microbiology and histopathology, with a manager responsible for service, safety and quality. Staffing depends on workload, test menu, opening hours and national rules. Roles include laboratory director, section heads, medical laboratory scientists, technicians, phlebotomists and clerks. Training records and cover for absence keep the service reliable. Professional registration and staffing standards are country-specific, so check current national guidance.

sections.heading: Workflow and inventory
sections.text: Workflow is the path of a specimen from collection to report. Turn-around time (TAT) is the time taken, often from receipt to authorised result. Map each step, remove bottlenecks, and set priority rules for urgent samples. Inventory control keeps reagents and consumables available without waste. Procurement should use clear specifications, supplier checks and first-expiry-first-out stock rotation. A simple reorder point is average daily use × lead time + safety stock. For example, 50 tubes daily, a 10-day lead time and 100 safety stock give 50 × 10 + 100 = 600 tubes.

sections.heading: Information systems
sections.text: A laboratory information system (LIS) records orders, specimens, results, quality control and billing. It reduces transcription errors and supports TAT monitoring. Data security means controlling who can see or change records, keeping audit trails, backing up data and protecting confidentiality. National data protection laws and institutional policies differ, so follow the current local rules. Paper systems need the same discipline.

sections.heading: Budget and communication
sections.text: A budget is a plan of expected income and costs. Fixed costs do not change with test volume, such as rent; variable costs rise with each test, such as reagents. Cost per test = total cost ÷ number of tests. If annual cost is 48,000 and 12,000 tests are done, cost per test is 48,000 ÷ 12,000 = 4.00 currency units. Health economics compares costs with benefits, but local prices and funding rules vary. Communicate with clinicians through clear reports, reference intervals and prompt critical-result calls. Agree who is contacted, record the call and review complaints together.

keyPoints: Organise the laboratory by sections, with clear roles, training records and cover for absence.
Turn-around time is often measured from receipt to authorised result; map workflow and set priority rules for urgent samples.
Reorder point = average daily use × lead time + safety stock.
A laboratory information system supports orders, results, quality control and turn-around monitoring; protect it with access control, audit trails and backups.
Cost per test = total cost ÷ number of tests; fixed costs do not vary with volume, variable costs do.
Communicate critical results promptly, record the contact and review feedback with clinicians.

en.title: Diagnostic testing, test evaluation and clinical correlation
en.short: Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, reference intervals and safe test use.

sections.heading: Test performance
sections.text:
Sensitivity is the proportion of diseased people who test positive: true positives ÷ (true positives + false negatives). Specificity is the proportion of non-diseased people who test negative: true negatives ÷ (true negatives + false positives). Positive predictive value (PPV) is true positives ÷ all positives; negative predictive value (NPV) is true negatives ÷ all negatives. PPV and NPV depend on prevalence, so rare disease gives many false positives. The positive likelihood ratio (LR+) is sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity); the negative likelihood ratio (LR−) is (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity.

Example: of 1,000 people, 100 have disease. The test is positive in 90 diseased and 90 healthy people. Sensitivity = 90 ÷ 100 = 0.90. Specificity = 810 ÷ 900 = 0.90. PPV = 90 ÷ 180 = 0.50. NPV = 810 ÷ 820 = 0.988. LR+ = 9. LR− = 0.11.

sections.heading: Reference and critical values
sections.text: A reference interval is the range containing most results from a defined healthy population, commonly the central 95%, so about 5% of healthy people fall outside. It depends on method, age, sex and population, so laboratories should verify their own intervals. A critical value is a result so abnormal that it may threaten life and needs urgent reporting. Exact limits are set locally.

sections.heading: Point of care and stewardship
sections.text: Point-of-care testing (POCT) is testing near the patient, often by non-laboratory staff. It gives fast results but needs training, quality control and documentation. Diagnostic stewardship means ordering the right test for the right patient at the right time, and avoiding unnecessary tests that can cause false positives, cost and harm. Choose tests by pre-test probability, the chance of disease before testing, and follow local or WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Clinical correlation
sections.text: Always interpret a result with the history, examination and other findings. A positive result in a low-probability patient is often false; a negative result in a high-probability patient may be false. Ask whether the result changes management. Guidelines and limits change, so check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Sensitivity = true positives ÷ (true positives + false negatives); specificity = true negatives ÷ (true negatives + false positives).
PPV = true positives ÷ (true positives + false positives) and NPV = true negatives ÷ (true negatives + false negatives); both depend on prevalence.
LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity.
A reference interval usually covers the central 95% of a healthy population and should be verified locally.
Critical values are life-threatening results that need urgent reporting; exact limits are local.
Diagnostic stewardship means choosing tests by pre-test probability, avoiding unnecessary tests, and interpreting every result with the clinical picture.

en.title: Public health laboratory practice and surveillance
en.short: How laboratories support surveillance, screening, outbreak investigation and reporting.

sections.heading: Surveillance and screening
sections.text: Public health laboratory practice uses laboratory data to protect whole populations, not only individual patients. Surveillance is the ongoing, systematic collection, analysis and interpretation of health data, linked to action. Laboratories support it by confirming diagnoses, identifying pathogens and monitoring trends, including antimicrobial resistance. Screening means testing people who have no symptoms to find disease early. A screening programme needs a suitable test, clear follow-up and treatment, and quality assurance.
