WHO and national public health guidance set priorities; follow the current national protocol.

sections.heading: Notifiable diseases and outbreaks
sections.text: A notifiable disease is one that law or regulation requires doctors and laboratories to report to public health authorities. Lists differ by country and change over time, so check the current national list. The WHO International Health Regulations (2005) also require countries to notify WHO of events that may become a public health emergency of international concern. In an outbreak, the laboratory confirms the cause and characterises the agent. For example, after a funeral several people develop watery diarrhoea. Stool culture confirms Vibrio cholerae O1. Rapid reporting triggers water-safety measures and oral rehydration.

sections.heading: Referral networks and data
sections.text: Specimen referral moves samples from peripheral clinics to reference laboratories. It needs safe packaging, correct forms, chain of custody and tracking so results return to the right place. A laboratory network links district, regional and national levels with standard methods, quality control and feedback. Data reporting uses standard case definitions and denominators. For example, if 40 of 200 stool samples are positive, the positivity rate is 40 ÷ 200 × 100 = 20%. Report line lists and weekly totals promptly. In the WHO African Region, Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) guides this work; national protocols and WHO guidance should be checked for current requirements.

keyPoints: Surveillance is the ongoing collection, analysis and use of health data for action.
Screening tests people without symptoms and needs a suitable test, follow-up and quality assurance.
Notifiable disease lists differ by country and change, so check the current national list.
Laboratories confirm the cause of outbreaks and help guide control measures.
Specimen referral needs safe packaging, correct forms, chain of custody and tracking.
Positivity rate = number positive ÷ number tested × 100; report data promptly using standard case definitions.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and regulation in laboratory medicine
en.short: Consent, confidentiality, ethical dilemmas, competence, CPD, regulation and research ethics in laboratory medicine.

sections.heading: Consent and confidentiality
sections.text:
Consent is a person’s free agreement to a test or sample use. Valid consent needs information, understanding and voluntariness. Routine care may imply consent, but extra tests, teaching use and research usually need explicit consent. Patient rights include privacy, information, refusal and access to results.

Confidentiality means sharing results only with people who need them for care, quality or law. Explain legal limits before testing. Case: a scientist in Kano gets a positive HIV result for a student who asks that nobody be told. The scientist protects the record, follows national reporting rules, and does not gossip. If a partner may be at risk, the scientist refers to the team.

sections.heading: Dilemmas and competence
sections.text:
An ethical dilemma is a conflict between duties. Examples include an unexpected genetic finding, a critical result after hours, or pressure to change a report. Critical results must be communicated promptly by the agreed route. Reports must be accurate and never falsified. Errors must be disclosed honestly and reviewed.

Competence is the knowledge, skill and judgement to perform a task safely. Work only within your training and authorisation. Continuing professional development (CPD) is planned, recorded learning that keeps competence current. It includes courses, audits and reflection. Keep evidence for regulators.

sections.heading: Regulation and research
sections.text:
Regulation is country-specific. It covers registration, scope of practice, standards and discipline. In Nigeria, the Medical Laboratory Science Council of Nigeria (MLSCN) regulates the profession. In the UK, the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC) regulates biomedical scientists. In the US, the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA) set federal laboratory standards, and states may add personnel rules. Professional codes set duties such as honesty, confidentiality, competence and reporting concerns. Check your current national law, regulator and code.

Research ethics concerns right conduct in research. Human-sample research normally needs ethics committee approval, informed consent, privacy protection and honest reporting. Leftover samples need approved terms. Follow national and World Health Organization guidance.

keyPoints: Valid consent needs information, understanding and free choice, and extra tests or research usually need explicit consent.
Confidentiality is limited by law and public health duties, so explain the limits before testing.
Critical results must be reported promptly by the agreed route, and reports must never be falsified.
Work only within your competence and keep recorded evidence of continuing professional development.
Regulation is country-specific; check your national regulator, law and professional code.
Research on human samples needs ethics committee approval, informed consent, privacy protection and honest reporting.

en.title: Research methods, biostatistics and scientific writing
en.short: Study designs, sampling, statistics, critical appraisal, ethics and writing a laboratory research project.

sections.heading: Designs and sampling
sections.text:
Research methods are the planned steps for answering a question. Designs are observational (cross-sectional, cohort, case-control) or experimental (randomised controlled trial). Laboratory studies often compare a new test with a reference method. Sampling means choosing participants or specimens. Random sampling reduces selection bias; consecutive sampling is common but needs caution.

Define the population, inclusion criteria and sample size before data collection. Sample size depends on the question, expected difference, variability, significance level and power; use a recognised formula or statistician.

sections.heading: Data and statistics
sections.text:
Data collection must be consistent: pilot the form, calibrate instruments and record units. Descriptive statistics summarise data. The mean is the sum divided by the number of observations. The standard deviation (SD) shows spread.

For five haemoglobin values 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14 g/dL, mean = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 g/dL. Deviations from 12 are −2, −1, 0, 1 and 2; their squares sum to 10. Sample variance = 10 ÷ (5 − 1) = 2.5, so SD = √2.5 ≈ 1.58 g/dL.

Inferential statistics use a sample to judge a population. A p-value estimates the probability of the observed result, or a more extreme one, if the null hypothesis is true. A 95% confidence interval gives a range of plausible values. Choose tests such as t-test or chi-square according to data type and design.

sections.heading: Appraisal, ethics and writing
sections.text:
Literature searching uses databases such as PubMed. Critical appraisal asks whether a study is valid, what it found and whether it applies locally. Research ethics protects people and specimens: seek ethics approval, obtain informed consent where required, protect confidentiality, and follow national rules and laboratory safety.

A proposal states the background, question, aims, methods, analysis plan, timeline and budget. Referencing must follow the required style, such as Vancouver or APA, and every citation must match a real source. The final-year project is assessed on clear reporting, honest limitations and reproducible methods. Check current national and WHO guidance for health research ethics.

keyPoints: Choose the design and sampling method before data collection, and justify the sample size.
Mean = sum ÷ n; sample SD = √[Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)].
Use descriptive statistics to summarise data and inferential tests to generalise, interpreting p-values and confidence intervals cautiously.
Search databases systematically and appraise studies for validity, results and local applicability.
Seek ethics approval, obtain consent where required, and protect confidentiality.
Write a clear proposal and reference every source accurately in the required style.

en.title: Advanced research methods and biostatistics for the dissertation
en.short: Advanced designs, sampling, regression, missing data, appraisal, ethics and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: Design and sampling
sections.text:
Advanced designs answer specific questions. A randomised controlled trial allocates an intervention by chance to reduce confounding. A cohort follows exposed and unexposed people forward; a case-control compares past exposure in cases and controls; a cross-sectional measures exposure and outcome at one time. Cluster and stepped-wedge trials randomise groups, not individuals.

Sampling may be simple random, stratified, cluster or multistage. Probability sampling gives every unit a known chance of selection; convenience sampling does not. Sample size depends on the smallest important effect, variability, significance level and power, so calculate it before collecting data.

sections.heading: Regression and missing data
sections.text:
Multivariable regression estimates the effect of one variable while adjusting for others. Linear regression models a continuous outcome; logistic regression models a binary outcome and reports odds ratios; Cox regression models time to an event and reports hazard ratios. Report estimates with 95% confidence intervals, not p values alone.

Missing data are missing completely at random (MCAR) if missingness is random, missing at random (MAR) if it depends on observed variables, and missing not at random (MNAR) if it depends on the missing value itself. Complete-case analysis can bias results; multiple imputation is valid under MAR. Bias includes selection, information and confounding. For example, if 20 of 100 exposed and 10 of 100 unexposed develop an outcome, the risk ratio is (20÷100)÷(10÷100)=2.0, but confounding may explain part of it.

sections.heading: Protocol, ethics and writing
sections.text:
Write the protocol before starting. State the research question in PICO form: population, intervention or exposure, comparison and outcome. Give the design, sampling, sample size, analysis plan, data management and timeline.

Seek ethics approval and follow national governance rules; obtain informed consent, protect confidentiality and plan any specimen storage. Appraise papers for validity, risk of bias, effect size, precision and applicability. For the dissertation, keep a timeline, meet your supervisor, follow reporting guidelines such as STROBE for observational studies and CONSORT for trials, and write each chapter to answer the question, not to fill pages.

keyPoints: Calculate sample size from the smallest important effect, variability, significance level and power before data collection.
Multivariable regression adjusts for confounders; report effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals.
Risk ratio = (risk in exposed) ÷ (risk in unexposed); odds ratio = (odds in exposed) ÷ (odds in unexposed).
Missing data types are MCAR, MAR and MNAR; multiple imputation is valid under MAR.
Appraise studies for validity, risk of bias, effect size, precision and applicability.
Write the protocol, obtain ethics approval and follow STROBE or CONSORT reporting guidelines.

en.title: Advanced laboratory quality, accreditation and method validation
en.short: Quality systems, risk, validation, uncertainty, audit, EQA and ISO 15189 accreditation.

sections.heading: Quality system leadership
sections.text: A quality management system (QMS) is the documented set of policies, processes and resources that make laboratory results reliable. At master’s level you design it, not just follow it: set a quality policy and measurable objectives, define processes and responsibilities, provide competent staff and suitable equipment, and review performance through management review. Leadership matters because quality depends on culture, open reporting and resources, not only on a quality manager. The system should cover the whole path from request and specimen collection to reporting and retention.

sections.heading: Risk and method performance
sections.text: Risk management means identifying what could harm patients or invalidate results, estimating likelihood and impact, controlling the risk, and monitoring whether controls work. Method validation establishes performance for an in-house, modified or non-standard method: accuracy, precision, specificity, limit of detection and robustness. Verification confirms that a standard or commercial method meets its claimed performance locally. Measurement uncertainty (MU) quantifies the doubt about a measured value; the expanded uncertainty gives the range within which the true value is expected to lie. For example, a glucose result of 5.0 mmol/L with standard uncertainty 0.15 mmol/L gives expanded uncertainty 0.30 mmol/L at k = 2 (the coverage factor), so report 5.0 ± 0.3 mmol/L (about 4.7 to 5.3).

sections.heading: Audit and external assessment
sections.text: An internal audit is a planned, independent check of practice against the QMS and standards; it finds gaps and drives corrective action. External quality assessment (EQA), also called proficiency testing, compares your results with other laboratories on the same samples. Poor EQA performance should trigger investigation, not blame. Together, audits and EQA show whether the system works in practice.

sections.heading: Accreditation and change
sections.text: Accreditation to ISO 15189 is formal recognition by a national accreditation body that a medical laboratory meets international requirements for quality and competence. It is voluntary in many countries but may be required by regulators or purchasers; rules differ, so check current national requirements. Change management supports new methods, equipment or information systems through planning, communication, training, documentation and monitoring. Accreditation is a cycle of improvement, not a one-time certificate.

keyPoints: A quality system needs leadership, documented processes, competence and management review.
Risk management identifies hazards, assesses likelihood and impact, controls them and monitors effectiveness.
Validation establishes performance of in-house or modified methods; verification confirms a standard method locally.
Expanded uncertainty = k × standard uncertainty (k is the coverage factor); with k = 2, 5.0 ± 0.3 mmol/L means about 4.7 to 5.3.
Internal audit checks compliance; EQA compares performance with other laboratories.
ISO 15189 accreditation is granted by a national accreditation body and requires planned change management.

en.title: Molecular genomics and advanced diagnostics
en.short: Next-generation sequencing, variant interpretation, quality control, ethics and emerging genomic applications.

sections.heading: Sequencing and variation
sections.text: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) reads millions of DNA fragments in parallel. It can target selected genes, the exome (protein-coding regions) or the whole genome. Genomic variation includes single-nucleotide variants, small insertions and deletions, copy-number changes and structural rearrangements. A variant is described against a named reference genome, because the same position can have different coordinates in different builds. Test scope matters: a targeted panel finds less than a genome, but may be cheaper and easier to interpret.

sections.heading: Bioinformatics and reporting
sections.text: Bioinformatics turns raw reads into variant calls. Steps include base calling, alignment to a reference, variant calling, annotation and filtering. Pipelines and reference versions must be recorded. Clinical interpretation weighs population frequency, gene-disease evidence, functional data and inheritance. Germline (inherited) classification often follows ACMG/AMP-style frameworks (the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology); tumour (somatic) interpretation differs. A report states specimen, test, gene, variant, zygosity (one or both copies), classification, limitations and recommendations. It supports, but does not replace, clinical judgement. Worked example: if 30 of 1,000 reads at a site carry a variant, the variant allele frequency is 30 ÷ 1,000 = 0.03, or 3%. In tumour testing this may suggest a subclone (minor cell population); low-level calls need cautious review.

sections.heading: Quality and ethics
sections.text: Quality control for genomic tests covers sample identity, DNA quality, library preparation, coverage depth (how many reads cover a site), uniformity, contamination, controls and confirmatory testing. Validation must define the limit of detection and reportable range. External quality assessment and accreditation, such as ISO 15189 for medical laboratories, support reliability. Ethical, legal and social issues include informed consent, privacy, data security, incidental findings, implications for relatives, discrimination and equitable access. Laws differ by country, so check current national and institutional guidance. This is education, not medical advice.

sections.heading: Emerging frontiers
sections.text: Pharmacogenomics studies inherited variation that affects drug response, such as CYP2D6 and HLA alleles; current guidelines from bodies such as CPIC (the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium) and national regulators should be checked. Pathogen genomics uses whole-genome sequencing to trace outbreaks and detect resistance markers; WHO provides guidance.

keyPoints: NGS reads many DNA fragments in parallel and can target genes, exome or genome.
Genomic variants are described against a named reference genome build.
Bioinformatics steps include alignment, variant calling, annotation and filtering.
Variant allele frequency = reads carrying the variant ÷ total reads at the site.
Genomic tests need validation, controls, external quality assessment and accreditation.
Pharmacogenomics and pathogen genomics are growing applications; check current national or WHO guidance.
